title: The Six Strategic Goals: How the Bosnian Serb Assembly Chose War
content:
On 12 May 1992, the Assembly of the Republika Srpska convened in Banja Luka to formalize the war aims that would drive Bosnian Serb military and political strategy for the next three and a half years. With Bosnia-Herzegovina's independence referendum having passed on 1 March and international recognition following on 6 April, the Bosnian Serb leadership under Radovan Karadžić moved to codify a territorial vision that rejected the new state's legitimacy. The session produced what became known as the Six Strategic Goals of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

The six goals, as presented by Karadžić and adopted by the assembly, were explicit in their scope. The first called for the separation of Serb peoples from the other two constituent nations — Bosniaks and Croats. The second demanded the establishment of a corridor through the Posavina region in northern Bosnia, linking Serb-held territories in the west with Serbia proper. The third sought control of the Drina River valley, creating a contiguous border with Serbia along Bosnia's eastern frontier. The fourth aimed to establish the Una and Neretva rivers as natural borders of the Serb entity. The fifth called for the partition of Sarajevo into separate Serb and Bosniak zones. The sixth asserted Bosnian Serb access to the Adriatic Sea. Taken together, these objectives constituted a comprehensive program for redrawing Bosnia's internal geography along ethnic lines, implying the displacement of non-Serb populations from enormous swathes of territory.

The ICTY Karadžić Trial Judgment (IT-95-5/18-T) established that these goals were central to the joint criminal enterprise through which crimes against non-Serb civilians were organized and carried out across Bosnia. The judgment found that the strategic objectives, declared openly in a legislative chamber, provided the framework within which subsequent military campaigns, forced population transfers, and acts of persecution were planned and executed. The ICJ in its 2007 Bosnia v. Serbia judgment similarly treated the political declarations of this period as relevant context for its analysis of subsequent events and their legal character.

Also present at the session was General Ratko Mladić, newly appointed commander of the Army of Republika Srpska. Mladić addressed the assembly in terms that would later feature prominently in ICTY proceedings. He spoke with a bluntness that contrasted sharply with the political language of the assembly’s resolutions, warning that the military campaigns necessary to achieve the stated goals would be prolonged and devastating. His remarks were later cited in ICTY proceedings as evidence that the Bosnian Serb leadership understood, from the outset, the scale of violence their territorial program would require.

From the Bosnian Serb perspective, the goals represented the protection of a community that feared minority status within an independent, Bosniak-majority state. From the perspective of Bosniaks and Bosnian Croats, the same framework constituted an existential threat — a blueprint for ethnic cleansing dressed in the language of national self-determination. The significance of 12 May 1992 lies in its documentary clarity. The Six Strategic Goals were not inferred after the fact by prosecutors or historians; they were proclaimed openly, recorded officially, and pursued systematically. They remain among the most important documents for understanding why the Bosnian War unfolded with such geographic scope and demographic ferocity across so many fronts simultaneously.
